options: A bit pattern whose fields are the values particular wires need
A command the processor looks up and interprets
A name the decoder translates into operations
A sequence of microcode addresses
drills.why: The fields are not descriptions of what to do. They are laid out so the wires can be cut straight from the instruction register with no logic between.

drills.q: Where does a destination register field go?
options: Onto the select inputs of the decoder that produces the write enables
Into a table that maps numbers to registers
Into a comparator against each register's identifier
Into the arithmetic unit
drills.why: The field is not a name for a register, it is the number that lights that register's line. That is unit 006 arriving inside an instruction set.

drills.q: Why does keeping a field in the same place across instructions matter?
options: It makes the field a wire; moving it needs a multiplexer to find it
It makes the instructions easier to read
Assemblers require it
It has no cost either way
drills.why: And the cost repeats for every field and every instruction, which is why fixed layouts exist and why the machines designed when decoding cost most have the most regular ones.

drills.q: What pressure pushes against a fixed, regular layout?
options: Code size, since variable-length instructions let common operations be
Clock frequency
The number of registers
Power consumption in the decoder
drills.why: It mattered enormously when memory was small and matters again now, because instruction bytes travel through the same caches as everything else.

drills.q: What does one bit splitting the instruction set into families buy?
options: Neither half needs to examine the other's fields
Twice as many instructions
A shorter instruction word
Backwards compatibility
drills.why: Nothing else needs examining to know which half of the machine is involved, and it costs about two gates.

drills.q: The decoder for the non-arithmetic half is:
options: A small ordinary decoder, gated by the family bit
A lookup table in memory
A state machine
A microcode sequencer
drills.why: Three bits into a decoder is the entire non-arithmetic decode in Scott's machine. Not a lookup, not an interpretation.

drills.q: In a machine whose arithmetic unit has six control bits, the operation field is:
options: Those six bits, set directly by the instruction
An index into a table of eighteen operations
A name the decoder resolves
A pointer to microcode
drills.why: The instruction sets switches rather than naming an operation. The encoding and the circuit were designed together, and the field is the control word.

drills.q: What does putting a small memory between instruction bits and control wires buy?
options: The instruction set becomes data, so adding an instruction is reflashing
Faster decoding
Smaller instructions
Fewer control wires
drills.why: It costs a lookup. Wiring the bits straight through is cheaper and fixes the instruction set in copper, and which you choose decides what changing the machine means.

drills.q: Why can a sixteen-bit instruction not carry a fifteen-bit address and an opcode?
options: There is one bit left, which is not enough to say what to do with the
Addresses must be aligned
The instruction register is only fifteen bits
It can, using a prefix byte
drills.why: nand2tetris splits instructions into two kinds decided by the top bit, so addressing a location and operating on it are two instructions. That is why its assembly reads oddly.

options: Part of a single mnemonic that the assembler looks up in a table
An operator the assembler evaluates
A separator between operands
A hint to the optimiser
drills.why: Which is why such an assembler rejects M+D. It means the same thing arithmetically and is not in the table.

options: A list of names for bit patterns
A programming language with expressions
A description of what the hardware should do
Machine code with the numbers written differently
drills.why: The last one is nearly right and misses the point: the names exist for people, and there is no expression parser and no evaluation anywhere.

drills.q: The same byte reaching a printer, an instruction register and an adder means:
options: A letter, a jump and a number, and nothing in the byte says which
Three things the byte encodes at once
Whatever a type tag alongside it says
The same thing in three notations
drills.why: Each part was built with a code in mind, and once it was built the mind was gone and the code with it.

drills.q: Where is the table that maps byte values to letters?
options: Nowhere in the machine. It is an agreement held by people
In the printer's firmware
In the operating system
In a read-only memory on the processor
drills.why: There is a printer wired so certain patterns move certain parts. Calling those patterns letters is something we do, not something it does.

options: An AND of the bits that identify it
A comparison against a stored opcode
A lookup in the decode table
A dedicated comparator per instruction
drills.why: The control unit is a collection of those gates, which is why the next unit calls it the least clever component in the machine.

drills.q: Two parts of a machine reading the same bits differently happens because:
options: They are wired differently, and nothing in the bits distinguishes them
A tag bit tells each part what to expect
The decoder routes the bits to one part at a time
Only one part is powered at once
drills.why: Both readings happen at once, all the time, on the same wires. What makes one of them matter is which result gets captured.
